newsitem.title: USA: INSTANT VIEW - U.S. loses 40,000 jobs in Sept.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - U.S. loses 40,000 jobs in Sept.

text.p: Following are comments from U.S. economists after the Labor Department reported the U.S. economy lost 40,000 new jobs in September. The jobless rate, meanwhile, rose 0.1 percentage point to 5.2 percent.
U.S. economists in a Reuters survey had expected 166,000 new jobs to have been added to payrolls and a 5.2-percent jobless rate.

MATTHEW ALEXY, CHIEF MARKETS STRATEGIST, CS FIRST BOSTON CORP: "This is a good number for the (U.S. Treasury) market. It took the market a lot further than anybody expected. There are still issues that are concerns for the bears."
ALEXY continued: "The wage story is still there. The big story is will this filter into the (Producer Price Index). These numbers definitely show a bit of slowing in activity.
"The important thing to keep in mind here is that the pattern over the past few months was for private sector payrolls to move consistently lower.

"For the (Federal Reserve), there's another employment number before the next meeting. Our view has been that the Fed will be on hold for the rest of the year. This argues in the direction that the Fed will be on hold for rest of the year."
KEVIN FLANAGAN, VICE PRESIDENT AND AN ECONOMIST, DEAN WITTER REYNOLDS INC: "The wage pressures are something that you have to take note of right now.

"Actually, the rest of the report isn't as weak as it appears. A lot of it is just in the payroll part -- hours worked are up as well, the household survey shows some gains in civilian employment, but the markets, I respect, don't look at that ... but the Fed will," Flanagan added.

EVELINA TAINER, CHIEF ECONOMIST, INDOSUEZ CARR FUTURES: "(The Fed is) going to be relieved that the economy is slowing quite significantly. In fact, if you look at private payrolls, there's been a drop in August and another drop in September.

"The dilemma is that hourly earnings are not slowing down. In fact, they're picking up speed. So, the trend in hourly earnings is rising, while the trend in employment is falling. That's like the worst of both worlds to have. In terms of hourly earnings, we're not going to get any better news next month because the minimum wage went up October 1."

LACY HUNT, CHIEF ECONOMIST, HSBC MARKETS INC: "It's an indication that the underlying weakness in the economy is hitting the labor market and that the Fed is vindicated in not raising rates. I salute the Fed for its determination to hold off. It is good news for the Fed and good news for the bond market ... It does suggest there are more risks to the economy's stability than were previously recognized.
"Average hourly earnings are the caboose, not the engine. It is not a forward looking component, so I really am not that concerned about it," Hunt added.

DONALD MAUDE, CHIEF U.S. ECONOMIST, SCOTIA CAPITAL MARKETS INC: "There are a lot of aberrations in it. It's not as soft as it seems. Private payrolls were up 41,000. I would focus on that. Government (payrolls) were down 81 (thousand); most of that's teachers.

"You might see some (Gross Domestic Product) forecasts for the third quarter raised upward a couple tenths because of aggregate hours worked. Average hourly earnings were up five tenths. That maintains roughly a 3.5 percent year-over-year rate of growth. That is not a very comfortable number for the Fed."

SAMUEL KAHAN, PRESIDENT, A.S.K. FINANCIAL RESEARCH: "The overall number is weak. The message of all of this is that at least through September, things have been weak. There is weakness in the employment area in general. Government employment fell, but everyone expected that after overly strong government employment in the prior two months as teachers were added to payrolls. Even if you make those kinds of adjustments and focus on private employment, you still get a relatively slower trend in employment."
KAHAN continued: "People will want to see if that slowdown in employment will be translated into slower consumer spending.

"You did have a large increase in hourly earnings. But because this report does not adjust for changes in job occupations or payscales, we don't know if this represents an increase in wage rates or merely increased bonuses or a shift in jobs from low to higher-paying sectors of the economy. For that reason, the markets will focus on the upcoming Employment Cost Index to see if wage rates have really remained stable or whether they're accelerating.

"Though the non-farm payroll number painted a weak picture of the labor market, the other data do not portray as much weakness. The slight increase in the unemployment rate is probably not enough to remove concerns about inflationary pressures," KAHAN added.
